story.name: ジョニーの たび
story.title: The Lighthouse in the Fog
story.line: ジョニーが きりの とうだいの はなしを します
story.ja: ジョニーは列車で大陸を横断し、メイン州へ。灯台守のウォルトと冬をすごす。レンズみがき、らせん階段のペンキぬり、ロブスターロール。ある霧の夜、霧笛がこわれ、帰れない漁船のために古い鐘を鳴らしつづけ、船は無事にもどる。お礼に新しいコンパスをもらったその夜、ジョニーはやっとルースに手紙を書き、フェリーの話をぜんぶ伝えた。春、そのコンパスを持って帰る途中、嵐にあって……この島に流れついた。コンパスはまたなくなっていた。翌朝、ジョニーの姿はなく、砂に書きおきが残っていた。

segments.en: On the fifth night, more neighbors came than ever. Maple, Dom, and Goldie sat closest to the fire, with blankets over their knees.
Okay, last one. I'm kind of sad, honestly. I've gotten used to this. Same time every night, you know?
Me too, my dear. Me too. Now, where was I? Ah, yes. Maine.
From the desert, he took a long train across the whole country. Four days of farms and rivers and little towns going by the window.
At the end of it was a rocky coast, cold and gray and beautiful, and on the very last rock, a white lighthouse with a red roof.
Darlene's brother was named Walt. He was tall and quiet and had a beard like a winter storm. He shook Gulliver's wing and said, you're late.
I said, I'm a sailor, Walt, I'm always late. And he laughed. Just once. I found out later that's about once a month for Walt.
The work was simple, but there was a lot of it. Gulliver cleaned the big glass lens until it sparkled.
And he painted the spiral stairs, all one hundred and twelve of them.
A hundred and twelve stairs? Every day? Dude, that's a serious leg workout. I'm kind of jealous.
On Sundays, Walt drove them into town for lobster rolls. Big pieces of lobster in a buttered, toasted bun, eaten on a bench by the harbor.
Walt said, you don't eat a lobster roll inside. It's against the rules. So we sat outside and froze, and it was wonderful.
Then one February night, the fog rolled in, so thick you couldn't see your own feet. And the old foghorn coughed once and went quiet.
Walt listened to the radio and frowned. A small fishing boat was still out there. The captain couldn't find the harbor in the fog.
Oh no. That's so scary. Couldn't they just follow the light from the lighthouse?
That's what I thought, too. But in fog like that, the light just disappears. You can't see a thing. But you can still hear.
There was an old brass bell on the rocks below the lighthouse, from the days before electric foghorns. Walt handed Gulliver the rope.
Walt stayed on the radio, telling the captain to steer toward the sound. And Gulliver rang the bell. Slow and steady, again and again.
I rang that bell for two hours. My arms were shaking. I sang every sea song I know, just to keep the rhythm.
And then, out of the white, they saw two small lights, red and green. The fishing boat came around the rocks and into the harbor, safe.
The next morning, the captain came up the hill with a bag of fresh fish and a small wooden box. Inside the box was a brand new compass.
He said, a sailor should always know the way home. And I almost cried for the second time on this trip. Bottomless coffee was the first.
That night, he finally wrote to Ruth and told her all about the ferry.
When spring came, Gulliver said goodbye to Walt and got on a ship heading south, with the new compass safe in his pocket.
And then, of course, there was a storm. A big one. The kind sailors tell stories about.
And the next thing he knew, Dom was standing over him on the beach.
Wait a sec. So where's the new compass? The one from the fishing captain?
Gulliver patted his left pocket. Then his right pocket. Then the inside of his cap. He looked up at everyone with a very small smile.
Well. It seems I've lost it again. But you know, I'm starting to think that's not such a bad thing.
Everybody laughed, and the fire popped, and for a while nobody said anything. They just watched the sparks go up into the dark.
In the morning, Gulliver was gone. There was only a long line of footprints going down to the water, and a message written in the sand.
It said, thank you for the coffee. Back soon. Probably by accident.
And the tide came in, slowly, and smoothed the sand, the way it always does. Goodnight.
